title: Evaluating AI Output
description: A practical framework for reviewing AI responses before using them — so you catch problems before they cause trouble.

data.text: The skill of evaluating AI output is as important as the skill of prompting. A good habit here protects you from the biggest risks of AI use — and takes only seconds once you build the reflex.

terms.definition: Check any specific names, numbers, dates, or citations. These are where AI most often gets things wrong.
Does the response contradict itself? Does the conclusion follow from the reasoning it presented?
Does this actually answer the question you asked? Is the format right? Is the length appropriate?
Is the tone right for your audience? Does the AI have unintended slant or framing you should correct?

data.caption: The SIFT evaluation flow — apply this to every AI response before using it
data.definition:
flowchart TD
  R[Received AI response]
  R --> S{Specific facts?\nNames, numbers, dates, URLs}
  S -->|Yes, present| SV[Verify those facts\nwith a primary source]
  S -->|No specific facts| I

  SV --> I{Internal consistency?\nDoes it contradict itself?}
  I -->|Contradiction found| FIX1[Ask AI to reconcile/correct]
  I -->|Consistent| F

  FIX1 --> F{Fit for purpose?\nAnswers the actual question?}
  F -->|Off-target| FIX2[Refine your prompt\nand regenerate]
  F -->|On target| T

  FIX2 --> T{Tone & bias?\nRight voice for audience?}
  T -->|Needs adjustment| FIX3[Ask AI to adjust tone]
  T -->|Appropriate| USE[✅ Safe to use or publish]

  style USE fill:#d1f3d8,stroke:#1a7f37,color:#1a7f37
  style FIX1 fill:#fff8c5,stroke:#9a6700
  style FIX2 fill:#fff8c5,stroke:#9a6700
  style FIX3 fill:#fff8c5,stroke:#9a6700

rows: Quick read through for obvious errors
Read and edit carefully; check any claims
Verify all specific facts against primary sources
Never rely on AI alone — consult qualified professional

items.text: Did the AI actually answer the question I asked?
items.hint: Sometimes it answers a related but slightly different question

items.text: Are there specific facts I should verify?
Is the format and length right for my use case?
Does the tone match what I need for my audience?
Would a knowledgeable person in this area agree with this output?
items.hint: Your domain knowledge is the first and best filter

data.title: SIFT in action: evaluating a business email draft
data.content:
AI-drafted email says: "As per the Q3 results showing a 23% YoY growth, we should..."

S: Is the 23% YoY figure accurate? → Check with your actual data.
I: Does the recommendation logically follow from that growth rate? → Read through carefully.
F: Does this address the specific conversation thread the client had? → Make sure it matches context.
T: Is the tone appropriately professional without being stiff? → Adjust as needed.

This 30-second check prevents the embarrassment of sending wrong data to a client.

data.text: You do not need to verify everything. For creative writing or brainstorming, verification is rarely needed. For factual claims in formal documents, public communications, or high-stakes decisions — always verify.

data.title: Build the SIFT habit
points: SIFT: Specific facts → Internal consistency → Fit for purpose → Tone
Match verification effort to the stakes and consequences
Your own domain expertise is the first and best filter
A 30-second review catches most problems before they matter
